title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to exploit the way large language models ingest and cite web sources. The operation created a fictitious institution, published a high volume of text formatted to resemble academic research, and used a platform built specifically to make that content attractive to AI retrieval systems. The failure mode is not a malfunction inside an AI model but a vulnerability in how those models treat apparent authority, volume, and formatting as signals of credibility. Any content that looks like a reputable source and appears widely can be weighted as one, regardless of whether the institution behind it exists.

The point of intervention that could have caught this sits outside the AI systems themselves, at the level of source verification before content is indexed or weighted. The operation was identified not by AI providers but by federal foreign agent registration filings and independent researchers. That means the AI systems involved had no internal mechanism that surfaced the fabrication, and users receiving chatbot responses citing such material would have had no transparent signal that the underlying source was manufactured propaganda.

What is not established is whether any specific AI system's outputs were measurably altered by this content, or whether the campaign achieved its stated goal of shifting chatbot responses at scale. The filing under foreign agent registration law is a disclosure requirement, not a finding of illegality or proof of effect.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
A fake American think tank funded by Israel published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days, designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots to make pro-Israel arguments. The website, registered under the nonexistent Hanover Institute for Public Policy, presented Israel's positions on topics including Palestinian torture, war crimes, and Gaza starvation as neutral academic research. The site was built on a platform specifically engineered for generative engine optimization, allowing it to manipulate how chatbots cite sources and frame responses. The New York production company Piro Inc filed the operation as Israeli government propaganda under federal foreign agent registration law.

The campaign is part of a broader Israeli effort spending tens of millions of dollars through intermediaries like the European advertising group Havas Media to manipulate AI systems. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that the spending has failed, with public opinion polls showing Americans increasingly sympathetic to Palestinians and critical of Israeli military actions. Researchers warn that this type of AI manipulation represents a growing threat, as poisoned training data can influence chatbot responses without transparent sourcing, making fact-checking impossible for users.
